newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU slipping badly in eastern Germany.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU slipping badly in eastern Germany.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) are losing popular support in eastern Germany and could end up behind the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) there in next year's election, pollsters say.

The CDU, which sealed victories in the past two national elections with strong showings in the ex-communist east, fell behind the SPD in opinion surveys early this year and there are few signs of a change on the horizon, they said.

While it is too early for bets on Kohl's unprecedented bid for a fifth term in the September 1998 vote, CDU strategists in Bonn say they are concerned about the chancellor's fading popularity among his one-time strongest supporters.

Kohl's razor-thin majority -- his centre-right coalition has 0.3 percentage points, or 12 seats, more than the combined opposition -- means minimal shifts in voting patterns could threaten his government.
"Everything points to the SPD ending up a bit ahead of the CDU in the east," said Willy Koch of the Institute for Market Research in Leipzig.

"The CDU's early victories in eastern Germany were a surprise because they didn't have the sociological base here," Koch said. "Workers voted CDU in the east, unlike in the west. But this exception is passing."
Richard Hilmer, director of the Infratest polling group in Berlin, also saw CDU support sliding and said: "It will certainly be more difficult for Kohl this next time."
Hans-Reinhard Guenther, director of the Institute for Market Research, said the turn away from the CDU became clearly noticeable in polls early this year.
The CDU, which won 38.5 percent of the eastern vote in the 1994 election, has fallen from 33.3 percent in January to 27 percent in June, his institute's surveys show.
The SPD, which limped in at 31.5 percent in 1994, has risen from 30.3 percent in January to 37 percent in June.
Infratest's surveys show the CDU has slid from 36 to 28 percent while the SPD rose from 34 to 42 percent from January to July.

The two main parties are much closer on the national level. The latest Emnid survey this week showed the SPD at 37 percent and CDU at 36 percent. The Social Democrats won 36.4 percent of the national vote in 1994 and the CDU 41.4 percent.

As in the west, a main eastern voter complaint is Germany's continued record unemployment, which rose to 4.37 million in June -- 11.4 percent of the workforce -- and is expected to stagnate around that level next year.
Joblessness fell in western Germany last month but kept rising in the east. Overall unemployment is roughly twice as high in the east as it is in the west.

The polls show the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), reform successor to East Germany's communist party, has stabilised as the region's third political force with support ranging from 16 to 22 percent. Western politicians originally thought the PDS would just fade away in the post-communist era.
"I don't see it falling much between now and the general election," said Koch in Leipzig. "In the longer term, PDS support could even grow."
Kohl's liberal partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), have slid from the dismal 3.5 percent they won in 1994 down to about two percent. "They're hardly measurable," Guenther remarked.

The Greens, which in east Germany include the grassroots activists who led the 1989 popular revolt against communism, have moved up from the 4.3 percent they won in 1994 to between six (Infratest) and nine (Market research) percent.
Gerhard Schroeder, the Lower Saxony state premier competing with SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine for the nomination to challenge Kohl, is running far ahead in popularity polls.
In a Market Research poll about favourite candidates, Schroeder led the pack with 30 percent compared to 16 percent for Kohl and 10 percent for Lafontaine.
